entry.title: What Smooths Knowledge Work
entry.content:
I got the idea for this piece from the trousers maker Fusein, who lives in Japan and develops trousers under the brand Fuseinatti.

His products are classically cut and relatively wide. They are meant to look good and feel comfortable. The cut pays attention to what happens in typical body movements: Where does friction arise between skin and fabric? Where does the cloth pull or press unpleasantly?

In that case, friction is unwanted. Tight trousers can already bother you when you sit down, because fabric moves more strongly against the skin. The cut can reduce that. Extra layers of suitable material can too.

Engineering knows the same principle more clearly. Between moving parts of a machine, oil does the work. It lets components run against each other more easily and wastes less energy. What you need is an intermediate layer.

The same applies to communication and to how companies handle knowledge. Friction there often means coordination cost: searching, asking, waiting. What smooths that, I will call transparency below.

Friction in communication

That Fusein pursues this principle in Japan may be no coincidence, at least if you stretch the idea a little.

Japanese communication is often described as especially polite, careful, and considerate. Everyday forms aim to avoid open confrontation and thus social friction: refusal more indirect, criticism softer, meaning carried by gestures, pauses, or context rather than by the literal sentence.

That can work well in social life. It has a downside. Anyone who wants to avoid friction at all costs can create new friction. What feels more polite can lead to misunderstandings for someone who does not know the conventions. Avoiding friction does not solve every problem.

Friction may sometimes arise

In Germany, direct communication is often valued more highly by comparison, especially at work. Openness is seen as desirable, even when it feels uncomfortable at first. That can create conflict that leads to productive discussion.

For communication, what matters is that the friction serves a purpose. Productive friction can be necessary. Avoidable friction is waste.

Same metaphor, different type: with knowledge in companies, the issue is rarely productive confrontation. It is coordination friction. Employees hunt for information that sits somewhere in a system or in someone’s head, and they lose time. That ties in with Knowledge as a Business Asset.

Friction as a cost factor

Suppose an employee needs information for his work. The company has it. He still cannot get to it.

Perhaps he lacks permission for a document. Perhaps nobody knows where the information is stored. Perhaps only one person knows the answer. Perhaps there is no documentation and he has to ask around among colleagues.

In all these cases friction appears: send a request, wait, get forwarded, maybe the colleague is on leave. That is annoying and expensive.

Search costs appear, plus waiting time and dependencies. Mental load rises when someone again and again does not know where information lives or whom to ask. Across many employees and many tasks, that adds up to substantial effort.

What smooths the work is transparency

As oil sits between machine parts, handling knowledge needs an intermediate layer. For me that layer is transparency.

For work to run with as little friction as possible, it must be clear which knowledge exists, where it lives, who can access it, why certain rules apply, and whom to ask when your own access is missing.

Missing access needs transparency too

That does not mean releasing every piece of information to everyone.

Data protection, trade secrets, personnel data, and other sensitive content need boundaries. Restrictions can be transparent as well.

An employee should be able to see which kinds of knowledge his role can access and which areas stay closed. If information is unavailable, it should be clear, where sensible and safe, that this is a deliberate restriction and not an oversight.

The goal is maximum clarity about openness and its limits. Not openness at any price.

Not every friction must be removed

Friction is not bad by default, neither in communication nor in engineering. It is also what lets a car brake.

The same holds in companies. Not every question is unnecessary. Not every piece of information must be available to everyone at once. The problem is avoidable friction. Spotting it and removing it is a mark of good knowledge management.
entry.summary: Gatekeeping knowledge creates friction; sharing reduces it. Transparency is what smooths the work: clear what exists, where it lives, and what you may know.

entry.title: Knowledge as a Business Asset
entry.content:
Knowledge is everywhere in a company. In a simplified sense, everything starts with knowledge. An entrepreneur knows something, grasps a connection, or has a particular insight and turns it into a business model. He may know how a product is made. He may know a market, legal frameworks, or operational routines. The business model itself may even consist of selling knowledge, for example through consulting or training.

That knowledge lives in books, products, software, and machines. It shows up in processes and work instructions. And it sits in employees’ heads: techniques, exceptions, connections. From the sum of these skills, something emerges that customers will pay for. For every company, knowledge is a fundamental resource.

What is a company actually buying?

Take a software developer. Why does a company hire him? Because it needs someone who builds software. What does that mean?

The company is not only buying working time. It is buying the ability to solve certain problems with software: knowledge and experience. The developer knows how software is designed, programmed, tested, operated, and evolved.

In return, the company provides capital, infrastructure, customers, sales channels, and organization. Out of these resources comes a product with economic value.

The exchange looks simple at first. It becomes interesting during the collaboration. The developer does not only bring knowledge. He also acquires new knowledge.

Knowledge takes shape inside the company

At work, the developer learns the products, customers, industry, and internal routines. He learns which decisions were made in the past and why things are built the way they are today. Eventually he knows the codebase, the tools, the release and deployment flows, and the edge cases that only apply under a particular condition.

Much of this arises on the side: in meetings, old tickets, conversations with colleagues. This knowledge is potentially valuable for the company. It emerged through shared work and is tightly bound to the company’s products and organization.

So does this knowledge belong to the employee or to the company?

When knowledge lives in only one head

Imagine the developer leaves. Code, servers, and the development environment remain, of course. He may even have left solid documentation of his code. A gap still opens where knowledge was never written down: Why was one part of the application implemented this way? Why does a customer need a special arrangement? Which seemingly harmless change already caused problems in the past?

The knowledge has not disappeared. It is scattered across emails, tickets, pull requests, or documents on a work computer. Above all, it often remains in the former developer’s memory, a place the company effectively cannot enter.

The company paid for working time, infrastructure, and product development. Yet it may never have moved a substantial share of the knowledge created along the way into its own organizational sphere, and it can now take a hit. How is that possible?

An unusual way to treat an asset

With other resources, hardly anyone would accept this. A server an employee takes home after work. A machine with no inventory record, whose location no one knows after the person responsible has left. No one would entertain those ideas, because they would simply be negligent.

With knowledge we behave differently, oddly enough, because we can grasp it only indirectly. That does not make it less valuable. On the contrary. Trouble begins when companies organize their intangible resources more poorly than their material ones.

The decisive question is: Which knowledge is so relevant for the company that it must not remain tied to a single person indefinitely?

Put differently, a company must be able to run its critical processes even when individual people are missing. Without that kind of organizational resilience, knowledge loss hangs over every firm like a sword of Damocles.
entry.summary: Companies hold knowledge assets, often without inventorying them. Why knowledge is a critical resource, and which question organizations need to settle first.

entry.title: Pass Knowledge On – Or Start From Scratch

link.title: Pass Knowledge On – Or Start From Scratch

entry.content:
My first blog post on documentation and knowledge management was deliberately romanticized. I wanted to point out that it is easier to document something, to put it into writing, when you can imagine someone on the other end who could benefit immensely from the knowledge you have put into writing and would probably be very grateful for it.

Yes, where would we be as humanity if there weren’t always people who felt the urge to share their knowledge, to make it available to others, without even asking for anything in return?

Of course, not everyone is that idealistic, but they don’t have to be. In a company, the obvious goal is to make a profit, and knowledge is hopefully, like any other part of the company, a consciously maintained and curated resource. At the same time, a lot of knowledge is created within small circles and is only passed on within those circles. It serves to keep that circle alive. But even that requires some kind of motivation, a willingness, or simply a value that people see in it.

This makes me think back to my time as a student at the University of Freiburg, at the small Slavic Studies department and its student association. When I arrived at the university, my impression was that the student association essentially didn’t exist.

For those who don’t know: a student association is the usual framework for students within a department to organize themselves and represent their interests within the department.

Over the course of several years, students gradually built the student association up from practically nothing and established and re-established events for themselves and the other students in the department. These included, above all, orientation week for new students, as well as the summer and winter parties.

There was a hard core of people who always took care of things, and they naturally attracted other students who might not otherwise have taken the initiative themselves. Naturally, this meant that experiences were accumulated and refined from semester to semester.

But, oh dear, the time was approaching when the hard core would leave the department. At some point, student life has to come to an end. And, oh dear, oh dear, it looked as though there would be no new hard core ready to take over the reins and carry on the work of the student association. I didn’t want our work to have been in vain – for us to have rolled the boulder uphill like Sisyphus, only for it to come rolling back down again in the end.

So, to me, it seemed obvious that we should write down the experiences of the previous years, so that they might eventually find their way to motivated people – perhaps only after one, two, or three semesters – who would see it as their responsibility to carry on the old traditions and prevent a break in continuity.

Ironically, the COVID era began shortly afterwards. I had finished my studies, and, to be honest, I don’t know what happened after that. Most likely, the break I had anticipated eventually happened, and the boulder came rolling back down the hill.

Unfortunately, we never finished the documentation either. But I can very well imagine that, by now, there has been someone at the Slavic Studies department who wished they could have found something left behind by their “ancestors.” Perhaps then they wouldn’t have had to start from scratch, but could have built on the experiences of previous generations.

The first thing about knowledge that isn’t written down: eventually, it’s gone – and someone has to start almost from scratch again.
entry.summary: Why sharing knowledge matters: so others can build on what came before instead of having to start from scratch all over again.

entry.title: The magic of documenting
entry.content:
For many people, documenting sounds like grey forms and a tiresome duty. I want to invite a shift in perspective.

Let us treat documenting as something magical: something that allows us time travel.

What actually happens when we document? People turn an experience into information, give a moment a form, and hold on to something that had only just been unique to that moment. A note. A photo. A set of instructions. A book. A map. Suddenly something bound to a particular person and a particular instant can leave that instant and become reachable for others.

This happens in the large and in the small. Sacred texts outlast their authors. Histories let past events resurface. A researcher writes in a journal. Whether a few lines or whole books, the gesture is the same. Something is meant to remain for others. Knowledge moves from one mind to the next, from one moment to the next, across years or millennia.

Long before anyone called it “documentation”, people were making such time travel possible. Documentation connects two points in time that would otherwise have nothing to do with each other. That is why we can read documentation as an invitation to someone we do not know, or who does not even exist yet. To that someone we can say: this is what I lived, this is what I experienced, this is what I learned, and if you want, you can continue from here.
entry.summary: Documenting as time travel: turn experience into form, leave a trace, and invite someone unknown or not yet here to continue. In the large and in the small.
